title: Orbits; Dark matter and dark energy; Detection of exoplanets
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: A04-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; C05-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; C05-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; C05-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: C05-1#N.2, X-RADIAL-VEL-1#N.3, C05-1#N.6, X-RADIAL-VEL-1#N.6, X-RADIAL-VEL-1#N.9, X-RADIAL-VEL-1#N.10.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Rotation curve
items.clue: Graph of v against r for the stars and gas of a galaxy.

items.label: Centripetal force
items.clue: Role played by gravity for a satellite moving in a circle.

items.label: Period
items.clue: T for one trip around a planet; its square is proportional to r³.

items.label: Orbital speed
items.clue: Value of v for a satellite, fixed by GM and r; greater on a smaller circle.

questions.stem: A comet moves around the Sun in a highly elliptical orbit. Which statement about the comet agrees with Kepler's laws?

options.text: It moves at the same speed at every point of its orbit.
It moves fastest when it is furthest from the Sun.
The Sun is at the centre of its elliptical orbit.
It moves fastest when it is nearest the Sun.

questions.stem: The Sun (mass 1.99 × 10³⁰ kg) and Jupiter (mass 1.90 × 10²⁷ kg) are 7.78 × 10¹¹ m apart. How far is their centre of mass from the centre of the Sun? (Radius of the Sun: 6.96 × 10⁸ m.)

options.text: 7.4 × 10⁸ m, just outside the Sun's surface
7.8 × 10¹¹ m, almost at the position of Jupiter
Zero: the Sun is fixed at the centre
3.9 × 10¹¹ m, halfway between the Sun and Jupiter

questions.explanation: r = M_J d/(M_S + M_J) = (1.90 × 10²⁷ × 7.78 × 10¹¹)/(1.992 × 10³⁰) = 7.42 × 10⁸ m, a little more than the Sun's radius.

questions.stem: Tethys and Rhea are moons of Saturn, and their orbits may be taken as circular. Tethys has an orbital radius of 2.95 × 10⁸ m and a period of 1.89 days. Rhea has an orbital radius of 5.27 × 10⁸ m. What is the period of Rhea?

options.text: 3.38 days
2.78 days
4.51 days
6.03 days

questions.stem: The radial-velocity curves of two stars, P and Q, in a binary system have the same period. Star P's curve has an amplitude of 40 km s⁻¹ and star Q's an amplitude of 120 km s⁻¹. The orbits are circular and seen edge on. Which statement is correct?

options.text: P has the smaller orbit, so P is the less massive star.
Q is three times as massive as P.
P is three times as massive as Q.
They have equal masses, as their periods are the same.

questions.explanation: M_P/M_Q = v_Q/v_P = 120/40 = 3. The slower star is the heavier one.

questions.stem: A star of mass 1.6 × 10³⁰ kg moves in a circular orbit seen edge on. Its radial-velocity curve has an amplitude of 25 m s⁻¹. Its planet's orbital speed is calculated to be 92 km s⁻¹. What is the mass of the planet?

options.text: 5.9 × 10³³ kg
4.3 × 10²⁹ kg
1.2 × 10²³ kg
4.3 × 10²⁶ kg

questions.stem: Stars A and B have equal masses. Each has one planet, much lighter than the star, with the same orbital period. Both orbits are circular and seen edge on. Star A's radial-velocity curve has three times the amplitude of star B's. How do the planets' masses compare?

options.text: Planet A has one third of planet B's mass.
Planet A has three times planet B's mass.
Planet A has nine times planet B's mass.
The planets have equal masses, since their periods are equal.

questions.explanation: Same star mass and period, so the same orbit radius and the same planet speed. M_p = M_s v_s/v_p, so M_p ∝ v_s: three times.
